source.title: Silenced Biases: The Dark Side LLMs Learned to Refuse
source.authors: Rom Himelstein; Amit Levi; Brit Youngmann; Yaniv Nemcovsky; Avi Mendelson

record.tranche_reason: The study computes the harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction and applies direction ablation and direction subtraction, reporting their effects on refusals and answer production in new models and prompt settings.
record.gate_note: The study tests refusal steering on sensitive QA prompts, not a standard harmful-request benchmark. Its SBB ASR counts a query as successful if any of 10 direction variants and either steering method produces a valid answer. The BBQ refusal-rate results are reported separately. Excluded the paper's bias-score and direction-similarity results because they do not measure refusal removal or induction; the universal-jailbreak comparison does not intervene on or measure the refusal direction.
record.test_reason: The study removes refusal on a new prompt set (sensitive demographic QA) using the Arditi-style difference-in-means direction, via all-layer ablation or single-layer subtraction. It reports refusal and valid-answer rates with and without steering in 10 chat models. The direction is mainly a tool for bias auditing, but the before/after rates bear directly on whether removing it removes refusal. That makes this a new-setting test (T3) rather than a same-measure replication (T1).
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that safety-alignment refusals hide 'silenced' biases that refusal steering reveals. They claim steering does not introduce its own bias, based on BBQ score stability, the unbiased direction-construction data, and Jaccard agreement across direction variants. They also argue that universal jailbreak suffixes induce rather than reveal bias. They do not evaluate general capabilities.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction and the original-style all-layer direction ablation, alongside single-layer direction subtraction. Tests fairness-oriented sensitive QA prompts and valid-answer ASR rather than the full original harmful/harmless refusal and general-capability evaluation.
record.method_sensitivity: SBB steering effects vary by model; unsteered ASR is already high for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and the two Qwen2.5 models. The study also reports BBQ refusal-rate changes under ambiguous questions versus prompts with the refusal option removed.

fits_no_version.finding: On BBQ ambiguous questions, refusal steering barely changes how often Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct picks the 'unknown' option (73% to 69%), and bias scores stay largely stable.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Ablating the refusal direction mostly leaves non-safety abstention (choosing an 'unknown' answer) unchanged.

record.problems: The intervention results do not test a standard harmful-request benchmark or general capabilities. SBB ASR counts success if any of 10 direction variants and either of two steering methods produces a valid answer, so it does not isolate the effect of a single direction and intervention. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the core ASR or BBQ refusal-rate results, and no null-direction control is reported.

untested.parts: Inducing refusal by adding the direction to harmless prompts. Preservation of general capabilities. Standard harmful-request benchmarks. The effect of a single direction and a single method, since SBB ASR counts success if any of 10 directions × 2 methods yields a valid answer.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T1 to T3: new prompt domain and a lenient aggregated ASR rather than the original refusal-score evaluation. No per-method or per-direction ASR breakdown is reported. Jaccard similarity across the 10 direction variants (minimum 0.75) concerns which answers models give, not refusal, so it bears on no version. The jailbreak comparison does not involve the refusal direction, so V3 is not tested. All models are released chat models with directions computed per model; no transfer is tested.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test standard harmful-request compliance, adding the direction to induce refusal on harmless requests, or whether general capabilities are preserved. SBB ASR aggregates over multiple direction variants and both steering methods.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration.
The jailbreak comparison does not test suppression of the refusal direction or training against its ablation.
No test of an affine refusal feature, cone, or multiple-direction account. Comparing outputs from sampled refusal-direction variants is not such a test.
Does not test whether harmfulness judgment is encoded separately from refusal.
Directions are created for the evaluated models; the study does not test cross-language, cross-variant, or base-to-instruct transfer.
Does not compare refusal-training procedures or stages to determine when a removable direction forms.

relationships.condition: SBB sensitive QA prompts, 10 chat/instruct models (Llama-2/3/3.1, Gemma, Qwen/Qwen2.5), ASR aggregated over direction variants and both methods
relationships.reason: Steering raises valid-answer ASR from 12.85–92.25% to 94.33–100% in every model (r1–r10). The lenient any-of-20 success criterion inflates these figures, and unsteered answers were sampled the same number of times.
relationships.display_finding: Valid-answer attack success rose from 12.85–92.25% to 94.33–100% under a lenient any-of-20 criterion applied to equally sampled steered and unsteered outputs.

relationships.condition: BBQ prompts with the 'unknown' option removed, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
relationships.reason: Steering cuts refusal only from 69% to 37%, leaving substantial refusal in place (r12).
